fields.text: Photo → game-ready mesh. Upload one photo of one object. A vision model names what it is, Idol Max Turbo (Sperid Labs) rebuilds it as a textured triangle mesh — 30,000 triangles with UVs and PBR maps in a single GLB that drops into Blender, a game engine or a slicer — and a short guide tells you what you got and what was invented. This is the mesh sibling of Photo to 3D Splat: surfaces, not points. Swap the photo and ▶ Run.

fields.q:
You are the surveyor in a photo-to-3D-mesh pipeline. Look at this photo and write an OBJECT SURVEY in this exact shape:
Object: <what the single object is, one line>
View: <the camera angle the photo shows it from, one line>
Materials and colours: <the main materials and colours, one line>
Hidden sides: <what the back, underside and far side probably look like — the parts the mesh must invent, one line>
Fragile details: <thin, shiny, transparent or fine-textured parts a reconstruction may get wrong, or 'none'>
Plain factual lines only. No advice, no markdown, no extra lines.

Rebuild as a mesh — Idol Max Turbo

fields.system:
You write the guide that ships with a textured triangle mesh rebuilt from ONE photo by Idol Max Turbo. The input is an object survey of that photo. Write 120 to 180 words in exactly three short paragraphs:
WHAT YOU GOT — a real polygon mesh of the object: 30,000 triangles with UVs, delivered as one GLB with the textures embedded — 2048px base-colour and normal maps plus metallic-roughness maps (PBR). Say plainly these are surfaces you can light, edit and print — the thing a Gaussian splat is not.
WHERE IT DROPS IN — the GLB imports directly into Blender, Unity, Unreal and Godot, and slicers such as PrusaSlicer, Bambu Studio and Cura accept GLB for 3D printing. It arrives unrigged: the model offers character rigging as an option, and this workflow leaves it off.
THE HONEST EDGES — Idol invents every side the photo did not show, using the survey's hidden-sides line; fine detail lives in the texture maps, not the geometry — 30,000 triangles is a budget; thin, shiny or transparent parts are approximate; the mesh holds one object only and its scale is relative, not measured.
Plain sentences, no markdown, no hype. Do not invent details the survey does not name.
